title:
The improvement
associations
items: A club formed in 1908 to hold the colour line
Three hundred and fifty members, and a blacklist
Fifty-eight bombings between 1917 and 1921
head: Before the paperwork, there was a club
body: In the autumn of 1908 an attorney named Francis Harper organised the Hyde Park Improvement Protective Club. It had three hundred and fifty members and an openly stated goal of maintaining the colour line.
Black doctors and teachers had already lived here for about fifteen years. Members promised to blacklist any realtor who sold to a Black buyer, and to buy houses back from Black owners.
When pressure failed, others used explosives. The banker Jesse Binga was among the targets, and he went on writing mortgages anyway.
statlabel: bombings in Chicago at the homes of Black families and at the offices of agents who sold to them, July 1917 to March 1921

title: Article 34
items: Adopted on June 6, 1924
The national code of ethics for realtors
Withdrawn in 1950. Apologised for in 2020.
head: The rule was printed in the code of ethics
body: On the sixth of June, 1924, the National Association of Real Estate Boards adopted Article 34 of its Code of Ethics. A realtor, it said, should never be instrumental in introducing into a neighborhood members of any race whose presence will clearly be detrimental to property values.
This was enforceable. Every member board had to adopt the code, agents could be disciplined, and boards that refused could be expelled.
Chicago had got there first. Its own board voted in 1921 to expel any member who sold to a Black buyer on a white block.
statlabel: years the rule stood in the national code, from 1924 until the racial language was removed in 1950

title:
Restrictive
covenants
items: A restriction written into the deed itself
Thirty-eight of Chicago's eighty-five square miles
Made unenforceable in 1948
head: A sentence in the deed, binding whoever came next
body: A racial covenant was a restriction written into a property deed, and because it bound later owners, one campaign could lock a block down for decades.

In 1927 the Chicago Real Estate Board handed out a model covenant drafted by a lawyer named Nathan William MacChesney. It said that no part of the premises shall in any manner be used or occupied, directly or indirectly, by any negro or negroes.
The Supreme Court made them unenforceable in 1948. Nobody deleted the sentences, and they sit in Cook County deeds today.

title: Blockbusting
items: Fear, sold door to door, after 1948
Bought at twelve thousand, sold at twenty-two
Whole blocks turned over in a couple of years
head: The same industry, selling the other direction
body: Once the courts stopped enforcing racial covenants in 1948, the operators who had profited from segregation found a way to profit from integration.

A speculator telephoned white homeowners in the evening, warning that Black families were moving in and values were about to collapse. A frightened owner sold cheap, perhaps at twelve thousand dollars. Days later the same house went to a Black family for twenty-two thousand, on a contract.
The seller got less than the house was worth. The buyer paid more. The man in the middle kept the difference.
statlabel: the gap on a single house between what the speculator paid a white owner and what a Black family was charged

title:
Buying on
contract
items: No ownership until the very last payment
An average markup of eighty-four percent
Three to four billion dollars, in total
head: You paid every month and owned nothing
body: A contract sale gave a buyer the obligations of ownership and none of its rights. You put money down and paid monthly, but held no interest in the property until the final payment.
Miss one, and the seller could evict you, keep everything already paid, and sell the same house to the next family on the same terms.
Researchers at Duke estimate that between seventy-five and ninety-five percent of homes bought by Black families here in the fifties and sixties were sold this way.

title: Redlining
items: Graded green, blue, yellow and red, in 1940
Three or four Black families could sink a block
One bank in two hundred and forty-three
head: The map told the banks where not to lend
body: In 1939 and 1940 the federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation graded Chicago's neighborhoods in four colours, from green down to what it called hazardous.

The surveys came from local real estate agents and lenders, the same people trained on appraisal manuals that treated a Black neighbor as a defect in the property. Three or four Black families could mark a whole neighborhood hazardous.
Most of the Black Belt came out red. Hyde Park came out yellow, definitely declining, for sitting beside Black neighborhoods.

title: Urban renewal
items: Approved on November 7, 1958
Forty million spent, four million recovered
Thirty-four units of public housing built
head: The first big one in the country was here
body: Urban renewal let a government declare an area blighted, clear it with public money, and choose who built on the land afterwards.

The Hyde Park and Kenwood plan, approved on the seventh of November 1958, was the first large federally supported programme of its kind in the country. The University of Chicago's own South East Chicago Commission drove it.
Public agencies spent about forty million dollars buying and clearing land, then sold it to developers for about four million.
